title: Large Archives

These tools help with archives too large to load at once: reading metadata without data, organizing directories, finding patches by ID, handling gaps, and processing patch by patch. They build on the [spool tutorial](spool.qmd).

```{python}
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

import dascore as dc
from dascore.units import s

patch = dc.get_example_patch()
spool = dc.get_example_spool()
```

# Metadata without data

[`PatchMeta`](`dascore.PatchMeta`) is everything a patch is apart from its data: coordinates, attrs and dtype. [`dc.scan_payloads`](`dascore.scan_payloads`) returns these for a file, so a patch's shape and extents can be read without loading samples.

```{python}
meta = patch.drop_data()
print(meta.shape, meta.dtype)

patch_again = meta.to_patch(patch.data)
```

`drop_data` and `to_patch` are inverses. Operations which only describe data, such as `rename_coords`, run on a `PatchMeta`; those which compute samples need a `Patch`.

# Path attributes

Directory names written as `key=value` become string attributes on index rows and loaded patches. Multiple pairs in one segment use `__`; path values override attributes stored in the file.

```{python}
root = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
data_path = root / "experiment=demo" / "cable=north"
data_path.mkdir(parents=True)
dc.get_example_patch().io.write(data_path / "patch.h5", "DASDAE")

partitioned = dc.spool(root).update()
assert partitioned.get_contents()["experiment"].iloc[0] == "demo"
assert partitioned[0].attrs["cable"] == "north"
```

Renaming a partition directory and calling `update()` refreshes path attributes without rereading file contents. Removing a path attribute may require rescanning the affected file so its stored value can be restored.

Only directories below the spool root are parsed; the root and source filename are not. Values remain strings and support the normal attribute selectors. When a path key matches a coordinate, bare `select` targets the attribute; use `_coords` for the coordinate. See the [directory index note](../notes/spool_index.qmd) for update and indexing details.

# Finding a patch by ID

File-backed `origin_id` values are indexed, so a recorded ID can locate its source without loading every patch:

```{python}
wanted = spool.get_contents()["origin_id"].iloc[0]
found = spool.select(origin_id=wanted)
assert found[0].attrs.origin_id == wanted
```

`data_id` is also indexed. Attribute queries match the stored source ID. A value trim clears the ID in presented contents because the loaded patch names the window it read and so carries a different value; sample selections defer it until loading. Built or chunked spools may have no `origin_id`, and moving a source invalidates its derived IDs until the directory is rescanned. See [Patch identity](patch.qmd#patch-identity) for the identity rules.

An empty ID after a file move is intentional: retaining the path-derived value would point at a source which no longer exists. Calling `update()` rebuilds the row from its new location.

# Filling bridged holes

A chunk never yields a patch holding a hole: without `fill_value` a hole ends an output however wide the `tolerance`. With `fill_value`, a `tolerance` wide enough to span a hole merges the patches on either side and writes the missing samples, so the output is an ordinary evenly sampled patch.

```{python}
from dascore.examples import random_spool

with_gaps = random_spool(time_gap=np.timedelta64(1, "s"), length=3)
filled = with_gaps.chunk(time=None, tolerance=300, fill_value=np.nan)
```

`tolerance` alone decides which holes are bridged: a hole it does not span separates patches as before, and nothing is filled across it. When a chunk length is given as well, the windows cover the whole bridged span, so one lying entirely inside a hole comes back as an all-fill patch and one the sources only partly feed is padded rather than left short. The fill value has to survive a cast to the data's own dtype, so `np.nan` needs float data; fill integer data with an integer, or cast it first. [`Patch.fill_gaps`](`dascore.Patch.fill_gaps`) does the same to a patch you already hold.

# Gaps and coverage

[`Spool.get_gaps`](`dascore.core.spool.Spool.get_gaps`) reports boundaries that `chunk` will not merge. [`Spool.get_coverage`](`dascore.core.spool.Spool.get_coverage`) summarizes the same compatible groups.

```{python}
gaps = with_gaps.get_gaps()
coverage = with_gaps.get_coverage()
```

```{python}
second_scale_gaps = with_gaps.get_gaps(tolerance=1 * s)
```

`gap_size` spans from the last sample before a gap to the first after it, so subtract one sample step for the missing extent. The `tolerance` argument, shared with `chunk`, controls which boundaries count. Pass another dimension as in `get_gaps("distance")`; `time` is only the default. Coverage uses patch envelopes; a patch with holes is one row, and the runs its index stores make its holes gaps like any other. `group_id` links coverage rows to their gaps.

At the default tolerance of 1.5 samples, one missing sample counts as a gap. A quantity or timedelta bounds the excess over one step in coordinate units instead: a spacing is a gap when it exceeds `step + tolerance`. Coordinates judge their own gaps by the same rule (see [coordinates](coords.qmd#declaring-a-grid-and-finding-missing-samples)). Overlaps are not gaps; coverage calculates the union of available spans.

Coverage groups use patch kind, dimensions, sampling rate, and coordinate structure. One metadata tag can therefore produce several rows when its patches cannot be combined safely.

Use [`Spool.viz.coverage`](`dascore.viz.spool.coverage`) or [`Spool.viz.calendar`](`dascore.viz.spool.calendar`) to plot these summaries.

# Loading ahead

Use [`Spool.iterate`](`dascore.core.spool.Spool.iterate`) to load upcoming patches in a background thread while processing the current patch:

```{python}
from contextlib import closing

with closing(spool.iterate(max_in_flight=2)) as patches:
    for current in patches:
        processed = current.detrend("time")
```

A positive window requires thread support; use ordinary iteration or `max_in_flight=0` in WebAssembly. The limit counts upcoming patches; the current patch and any retained results are additional. Closing the iterator releases its loading thread even if the loop exits early. Ordinary iteration stays synchronous. The [parallel processing recipe](../recipes/parallelization.qmd) also shows how to scan directory updates with a reusable process executor.

# Mapping

[`Spool.map`](`dascore.core.spool.Spool.map`) eagerly applies a function to every patch. Chunk first to control work size.

```{python}
def distance_max(patch):
    """Return each channel's maximum."""
    return patch.aggregate("time", "max")


mapped = spool.chunk(time=5, overlap=1).map(distance_max)
result = dc.spool(mapped).concatenate(time=None)[0]
```

`map` returns a list by default. Wrap it with `dc.spool(...)` to continue using spool operations, as above. Active runtime configuration is propagated to thread and process workers.

See the [parallel processing recipe](../recipes/parallelization.qmd) for executors and larger workflows.
